summary.text: The cell nucleus is a membrane-bound organelle found in eukaryotic cells, and it contains nearly all of the cell's genome.
It controls the activities of the cell by regulating gene expression, and its double-membrane envelope isolates its contents from the cytoplasm.
Small molecules and ions move freely through nuclear pores, while large molecules such as proteins and RNA must be actively carried across.

facts.label: Pores in mammals
facts.value: Between 3000 and 4000 pore complexes per envelope

facts.label: Nucleolus
facts.value: Best-known nuclear body; helps assemble ribosomes

items.prompt: A biologist assumes every eukaryotic cell has exactly one nucleus. Which cell type shows the assumption is wrong?

options.label: Mammalian red blood cells, which have none at all
Mitochondria, which carry a nucleus of their own
Single-celled yeasts, which keep two nuclei each
Animal body cells, which share one nucleus

items.explain: Eukaryotic cells usually have a single nucleus, but mammalian red blood cells have none and some cells, such as osteoclasts, have many.

items.prompt: A cell must bring a large protein into its nucleus. How does it get across the nuclear envelope?

options.label: It diffuses freely through the membrane like small ions
It slips through the gap between the two membranes
Through nuclear pores, actively carried by carrier proteins
It waits and enters whenever the envelope breaks apart

items.explain: The envelope is impermeable to large molecules, so they pass through nuclear pores with the help of carrier proteins.

items.prompt: A forensic lab wants the part of a cell that holds nearly all of its genome. Where should it look?

options.label: The mitochondria, which hold a small portion of the genes
The nucleus, home to most of the genes
The nuclear pores, which store the chromosomes
The cytoplasm, which carries the full genome

items.explain: Nearly all of the genome is in the nucleus; only a small portion of genes sits in the mitochondria.

items.prompt: A gene is read by the cell again and again. How is its DNA most likely packed?

options.label: Tightly, in the compact form called heterochromatin
Tightly, as constitutive heterochromatin at a telomere
Tightly, as facultative heterochromatin in one cell type
Loosely, in the less compact form called euchromatin

items.explain: Euchromatin is less compact and holds frequently expressed genes, while all heterochromatin is compact and infrequently transcribed.

items.prompt: A microscopist sees the outer layer of the nuclear envelope blending into a neighbouring membrane network. Which network is it?

options.label: The nuclear matrix
The inner membrane of a mitochondrion
The endoplasmic reticulum
The nucleolus

items.explain: The outer nuclear membrane is continuous with the adjacent endoplasmic reticulum membrane.

items.prompt: A neuroscientist counts nuclear pore complexes in a large Purkinje cell and in a small glial cell. What does she find?

options.label: The Purkinje cell has far more, around 20,000 against a few hundred
Both have the same count, between 3000 and 4000 each
The glial cell has far more, because small cells need more transport
Neither has any, since pores appear only in a few cell types

items.explain: Pore numbers vary considerably across cell types: small glial cells have a few hundred, while large Purkinje cells have around 20,000.

paragraphs.heading: The cell's control room
paragraphs.text: The nucleus is a compartment wrapped in membrane, found in the cells of eukaryotes. Its name is Latin for kernel or seed. It holds nearly all of the cell's genome and steers what the cell does by regulating gene expression. Most eukaryotic cells have one nucleus, but mammalian red blood cells have none and a few kinds, such as osteoclasts, have many.

paragraphs.heading: A double wall with gates
paragraphs.text: The nucleus is enclosed by the nuclear envelope, a pair of membranes that keeps its contents apart from the cytoplasm. Inside, a network of fibres called the nuclear matrix lends mechanical support. The outer of the two membranes is continuous with the membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum. Large molecules cannot cross the envelope on their own, so it is perforated by nuclear pores. Small molecules and ions pass through these freely, while larger ones must be actively carried through by carrier proteins.

paragraphs.heading: Inside the pores
paragraphs.text: A mammal's nuclear envelope has between 3000 and 4000 of these pore complexes. The count varies a lot by cell type: small glial cells have a few hundred, while large Purkinje cells have around 20,000. Each pore complex is built from roughly thirty different proteins called nucleoporins. A pore is 100 nm across in total, but the gap that molecules can freely pass through is only about 9 nm wide.

paragraphs.heading: How the DNA is packed
paragraphs.text: Inside the nucleus, DNA is arranged in chromosomes, long strands dotted with proteins such as histones that protect and organise it. A human cell holds roughly two metres of DNA. For most of the cell cycle this DNA sits in a DNA and protein complex called chromatin, while during cell division the chromatin forms well-defined chromosomes. Euchromatin is the less compact form and holds genes the cell uses often. Heterochromatin is more compact and holds DNA that is rarely transcribed.

paragraphs.heading: Size and the nucleolus
paragraphs.text: The nucleus is the largest organelle in animal cells. In many eukaryotic cells it takes up about 10% of the cell's volume, and in human cells it is roughly six micrometres across. It has no membrane-bound rooms inside, but it does hold nuclear bodies made of particular proteins, RNA and parts of chromosomes. The best known of these, the nucleolus, takes part in assembling ribosomes.

paragraphs.heading: Two surprises
paragraphs.text: Not every gene lives in the nucleus: a small share sits in the mitochondria instead. The immune system can also turn against the way DNA is packed. Antibodies to nucleosomes and other kinds of chromatin organisation, called anti-nuclear antibodies, are linked to autoimmune diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus. They have also been seen alongside multiple sclerosis.
